extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, law, and public affairs; scholars and informed citizens interested in legitimacy of government and resistance
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains normative criteria about when conquest, usurpation, tyranny, or alterations of the legislative justify loss of political legitimacy and lawful resistance. Focuses on conditions that make governments dissolved or subjects free to resist or form new legislatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conquest does not create hereditary title to others' land
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfying of damages of war scarcely gives the conqueror title to any country he shall conquer; the spoil of war (destruction of a few years' product) is not equivalent to perpetual inheritance of land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conquest may give temporary possession or reparation but cannot lawfully dispossess the posterity of the vanquished of inherited property. Money and movable riches have only 'imaginary value' and do not justify perpetual dispossession. Example: conquerors take little care to possess lands where waste land exists, and five years' product is not worth perpetual inheritance.

rubrics_metrics.name: No dominion over those who did not join the aggressor
rubrics_metrics.description: Over those who joined not in the war, and the posterity even of those that did, the conqueror hath, by his conquest, no right of dominion: they are free from any subjection to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a conqueror has physical power to compel, that force does not create legitimate title to govern those who did not consent or join in the war; if former government is dissolved they may form another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promises and obligations extorted by force are void
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises extorted by force, without right, cannot be thought consent, and thus bind not at all; whatever another gets from me by force I still retain the right of, and he is obliged to restore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the thief with a pistol: a person who yields under duress does not thereby transfer moral or legal obligation. Extorted promises do not transfer right or obligation because the law of nature binds only by voluntary prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conqueror's authority is limited to persons who actually aided the aggression
rubrics_metrics.description: The conqueror, if he have a just cause, has a despotical right over the persons of all that actually aided and concurred in the war against him, and a right to make up his damage and cost out of their labour and estates, so he injure not the right of any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reparations and punishments may be taken from active participants to compensate injury, but this does not extend to arbitrary dominion over the innocent or over posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children/minors of the conquered retain natural freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The children, whatever may have happened to the fathers, are freemen, and the absolute power of the conqueror reaches no farther than the persons of the men that were subdued by him, and dies with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since a father does not have power over the life or liberty of his child, his acts cannot forfeit the child's natural rights; conqueror's power cannot lawfully bind the children without their consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property granted by conqueror is nonetheless property by consent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the conqueror grants estates to persons and their heirs, whatever is granted is property to the grantee so far as it is granted; without a man's own consent property cannot be taken from him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grants and titles given by a conqueror, once conferred and occupied with consent, create vested property rights that the conqueror cannot arbitrarily revoke without destroying all voluntary contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usurpation lacks legitimate right and cannot convert into lawful rule without people's consent
rubrics_metrics.description: An usurper can never have right on his side; whoever gets into possession other ways than laws prescribe hath no right to be obeyed, though the form of government be preserved, until the people are at liberty and actually consent and confirm him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usurpation is a change of persons but not of the constitution; the usurper's authority is illegitimate until the people freely consent and confirm the new holder of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tyranny: exercise of power beyond right and for private advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyranny is the exercise of power beyond right, used not for the good of those under it but for the ruler's private advantage—when the governor makes his will the rule and acts for ambition, revenge, covetousness, or other irregular passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tyranny can occur in any form of government (monarchy, oligarchy, republic) and is distinguished from rightful rule by ends (public good) and by adherence to law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where law ends, tyranny begins
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever the law is transgressed to another’s harm, and authority exceeds the power given by law, tyranny begins; acting without authority may be opposed as invasion of another's right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceeding legal bounds is no less wrong in a king than a constable; illegal acts by authorities lose their legal protection and may be resisted as attacks on rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on obedience: sacredness of person does not justify unlawful acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Though in some countries the person of the prince is sacred and exempt from judicial censure, this does not prevent opposition to illegal acts performed by ministers or officers who exceed the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The king's personal immunity protects office and person but does not validate illegal commands; commissions cannot justify actions against the law and those executing beyond legal limits may be opposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance is only lawful against unjust and unlawful force
rubrics_metrics.description: Force is to be opposed only to unjust and unlawful force; opposing lawful authority in other cases draws condemnation and endangers polity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between resisting violent robbery (immediate threat to life) and seeking legal remedy for non-life-threatening wrongs; violent resistance is justified where appeal to law is impossible or inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-defense and prevention justify killing when life is imminently threatened
rubrics_metrics.description: If someone with a sword demands my purse on the highway (threatening life), I may lawfully kill; where life is in immediate danger, the law of nature permits defensive killing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with property disputes where legal remedies remain available; immediacy and irreparability (loss of life) justify extreme self-defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to resist when legal remedy is obstructed by those in power
rubrics_metrics.description: If unlawful acts by magistrates are maintained by the power they have, and remedies due by law are obstructed by the same power, the right of resisting is preserved and may extend beyond private cases when the majority are affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When legal channels are blocked by those committing the wrong, resistance becomes more justified; yet small isolated resistance is unlikely to succeed unless broader public is convinced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrent arbitrary practices and systemic signs justify public suspicion and resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: If people observe pretences of law but actions tending to arbitrary power (eluding law, favouring ministers who promote arbitrary ends, supporting religion to introduce tyranny) a long train of such acts may persuade the people that their laws and liberties are in danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systemic patterns (repeated experiments of arbitrary power, favouring agents who promote it) are indicators that resistance and reformation may be warranted to prevent enslavement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between dissolution of society and dissolution of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissolution of society (the political union) usually happens via foreign conquest, which dissolves the community and therefore the government; but governments can also be dissolved from within by fundamental changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the society is dissolved (scattered, conquered) the government cannot remain; external conquest and internal breakdown both can end the political unity that sustains government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alteration of the legislative constitutes dissolution of the government
rubrics_metrics.description: When the legislative is broken or dissolved, dissolution and death of the society follow because the legislative declares the will and is the soul that gives unity to the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legislative's constitution is the fundamental act of society; unauthorized persons making laws, or obstruction of legislative functions, effectively dissolve the government's legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific acts that alter the legislative and dissolve government
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative is altered (and government dissolved) when: (1) the prince sets up his arbitrary will in place of laws; (2) the prince hinders the legislative from assembling or acting freely; (3) the electors or ways of election are altered without consent; (4) the people are delivered into subjection to a foreign power; (5) the supreme executive neglects and abandons its charge so laws cannot be executed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of these enumerated failures removes the ability of the people to be governed by their chosen will and thus restores a state where resistance or reconstitution of the legislative is justifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Those who change or obstruct legislative processes are guilty of the greatest crime
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prince uses force, treasure, and offices to advance changes in the legislative under pretence of lawful authority, he is most capable of dissolving the legislative and thus guilty of the greatest crime against the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the prince can suppress opposition and is in position to manipulate institutions, his abuse in altering legislative processes is particularly dangerous and blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: When executive abandonment reduces the polity to anarchy, government is dissolved
rubrics_metrics.description: If the supreme executive neglects and abandons his charge so that laws cannot be put into execution, he demonstratively reduces all to anarchy and dissolves the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A government without enforcement of law is equivalent to no government; absence of administration of justice and public power makes the society revert to a state where people may reorganize governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: People's right to erect a new legislative upon dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government is dissolved by conquest, usurpation, tyranny, or internal alteration, the people are at liberty to provide for themselves by erecting a new legislative differing in persons or form as they find best for their safety and good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both remedial and preventive: people need not wait until wholly enslaved to act; they have a right to prevent tyranny and reconstitute legitimate authority when prior structures fail.
